NEW YORK.

The Rev. Richard S. Storrs, D.D., of Brooklyn,
was chosen President; vice presidents to the num-
ber of twenty-eight were chosen; trustees to the
number of twenty-four.

The officers appointed by the trustees were—
Corresponding Secretaries, Rev. Ray Palmer, D.D.,
Rev. CHRISTOPHER Cushing, D.D.; treasurer and
Recording secretary, Rev. N. A. Wilkins, D.D.

The meeting opened by the performance of the
following programme:

Organ voluntary—Mrs. Marion Christopher, organist;
"Glory to the Lord" recitative and chorus;
"The Messiah" Handel, Mr. Rock;
"Elijah," Sohn; "Dolly," Mrs. Emma Watson;
chorus Haydn;
and chorus "Holy Saviour" hymn; songs of the.

After prayer the choir sung "Joy to the World,"
from "Songs of the Sanctuary" and the Rev. Dir.
the chairman, then delivered an address. He bal-
anced it by saying that it was fitting that at this annual
reunion some pleasant words should be spoken;
But just as at the New England Thanksgivings, the
absent ones so here. While we may rejoice at our
reunion, our joy is not unsaddened for the absence
of those who are not with us. During the twenty
years of the existence of this society we have lost
many whose names are dear to us. The twenty
years have brought us great changes—Sebastopol,
Solferino, Sedan, Gettysburg, names that are
pivotal of the world's changes. Prussia has
emerged with its modern ideas. And what
of Rome, that has received such terrible blows?
The Vatican is only an empire. The weak,
feeble old man of Rome, illuminating his obnoxious
doctrines, reminds one of Mrs. Malaprop trying
to stop the Atlantic Ocean with her broom. The
speaker next alluded to the late war on the rebel,
its causes, its terrors, its effects. To the
memory of Lincoln he paid eloquent tribute. In
speaking of Congregational churches he said
that in 1854 there were only 1896 congregational
churches, whereas now there are 1895 churches of
that denomination. Twenty years more and the
gates of the twentieth century begin to open, but
what clouds will obscure our view! But our prin-
ciples shall live, whether under our name or under an-
other name. The morning cometh. Twenty years
hence and the young shall be old, and where shall
the old be? To those who may be our successors
we send the hail hereafter, and we hope for re-
union somewhere in the Kingdom of our Father,
where nothing shall be shaded.

Rev. H. J. Gaither was next introduced and
that gentleman delivered one of his happiest ad-
dresses, which was received in the most cordial
manner.

Rev. Dr. Hall was the next speaker. He said
he had been told that his main business at the
meeting was to say pleasant things and to tell all
the good anecdotes he could remember. But he
could not tell stories, owing to a precept incul-
cated upon him when he was a boy that he should
not tell stories. He felt particularly glad, how-
ever, to participate with his Congregational
brethren in their reunion. The speaker then paid
glowing tribute to the services rendered to
Christianity by eminent Congregationalists who
had gone before, and to the general ecclesiastical
and secular work done by the members of the Con-
gregational denomination. His remarks broach-
ing upon grand unity of all the denominations,
which were uttered in the reverend orator's best
and most earnest manner, were most kindly re-
ceived by the audience.

Some other addresses having been made the
meeting adjourned.

The Washington correspondent OF the st.
Louis Democrat, of the fourth instant, gives
the following interesting facts which were
! brought out in debate on the military bill
the day before:


The army bill was the regular order in
the House, and after MIR. Beck had made a
speech in favor Of paying the national debt
in greenbacks, which savored like an echo
from the Democratic platforms of five or
six years ago, there was little serious and
practical consideration OF the military es-
tablishment a1d the necessity OF MAINTAIN


ng it at its present strength. The pending


question was on reducing the appropriation


for recruiting, so as to let the force of en-


listed men drop down to $4,000, but not


enlsting enough during the coming year


to keep it up to the maximum standard OF
10000.


Some interesting facts were stated by


Mr. Gunckel in relation to the cost OF the


British army, from which it appears that
the soldiery is maintained for less than one


half the American soldiery - is better


housed, better clothed, and better fed, al
though not SO well paid.


Mr.. Wheeler, who had the bill in charge,


in answer to the complaints OF Western
and Texas members that more troops are


needed to defend the Indian frontier, said


that if such was the case the War Depart


ment had better 90 into the fine houses Of
Of11C1dlS IN w washington, LdAt OuJ IHc private
soldiers who were acting as servants, put
uniforms on them, and send them to the
frontier. This statement, thrown out with
good deal of force and significance, Gre
ated sensation.


Mr. Wheeler was asked how many soldiers
were thus detained as servants, but replied
that he had no facilities for learning that
other members did not possess.


Mr.. Potter supplied the information by
saying that he was informed that there
were over 1000 enlisted men in Washington,
and leaving the inference that their duties
were not of a military character; the Mill
tary Committee, which has cOmmendable
reputation for finding out things, will doubt
less be stimulated by Messrs. Wheeler and
POtter's statements to investigate the mat
ter.


Mr. Garfield argued in favor of the pro-
posen reduction of 5000 men, saying that
there were now 5000 soldiers east of the
Mississippi OF whom 1924 we're around New
York harbor, and 1000 on the Canada Dor
der, lille there was not single British
soldier on the other side of the frontier.


The result of the debate was that the APP
preparation Committee was sustained in its
effort to reduce the rank and file of the
army, and the method by which it is pro-
posed to effect it was made more direct and

What is it? It is the practice of self
denial for the good of others. This
principle stands at the opposite
pole of selfishness. It is the law-
born sentiment that delights in self-
sacrifice for the good of others. It is
that which always commands the ad-
miration of the world, who has so much
learned of the old classics as Leonidas
and his Spartan band who so nobly of-
fered themselves on the altar of In-
dividualism in the Pass of Thermopylae.
The old Revolutionary soldiers living
on trenches, carrying an empty
sleeve at their side, were esteemed
great heroes. Why? Because they
suffered for others. They counted not
their lives that they might win civil
liberty for the nation. This was a sub-
lime sacrifice. See this self-sacrifice in
the part of those who labor, suffer,
endure hardships, fear rail, through
many long weary years, all for the good
of their children. St. Paul was inspir-
ed with this sublime self-denial for the
sake of others. He said, 'It is good
to drink wine whereby
others might be strengthened.' Paul knew
that his drinking, even very moderately,
would encourage others to drink
immoderately; therefore he resolved
not to touch it—not to handle it or
taste it. The noble principle here is
stated: That practice which,
might be innocent to ourselves, should
be abstained from, if that practice en-
courages others to commence a course
that may finally ruin them. Is not this
principle applicable to wine-drinking?
